topic: gas chromatography peak identification
prohibition: I’d like to, but do NOT increase the split ratio—my sample volume is already scraping the lower quant limit. Increasing the split tanks sensitivity, and I can’t afford re-collecting surface water tomorrow.
plan: Nadia plans to identify the unknown peaks in her chromatogram by matching their retention times against a published library of retention times, assuming that retention times are universal values that will match regardless of who runs the analysis.
flaw: Retention times are not universal; they shift depending on the specific column, stationary phase, temperature program, flow rate, and instrument, so published values won't reliably match her peaks. She would need to run standards on her own setup or use relative retention times or mass spectra instead.

topic: soil infiltration test interpretation
prohibition: Just watch the water level while I recalibrate the ruler, but whatever you do, do NOT dump extra gravel into the ring—
plan: Fen plans to run the infiltration test by pre-soaking the rain-garden soil overnight and then measuring how fast the second pour drains, reasoning that this gives a cleaner, more consistent reading of the soil's true infiltration rate.
flaw: A pre-soaked soil measures the saturated infiltration rate, not the design-relevant rate for a freshly constructed bioswale, so the result will overstate how quickly the garden will accept the first storm runoff and lead to an undersized or poorly judged facility.

topic: preventing sample-label mix-ups
prohibition: Because Maeve’s on the satellite phone fighting customs. Come on, just don’t press the label hard—really, whatever you do, don’t use the freezer door as a sealing edge; that edge cracks the code.
plan: Orla plans to pre-label all the sample jars in permanent marker before heading out, writing each station code and depth on the lids so the crew can just grab the matching jar as each net comes up.
flaw: Permanent marker ink on jar lids smears or rubs off once the lids are handled with wet, solvent-soaked gloves and exposed to seawater and sun, so the codes can become illegible. Labels need to be on the jar body or on durable waterproof labels rather than relying on marker on the lids.

topic: survey validity and reliability checks
prohibition: Online calculators don’t help when your sample came from one union listserve. Don’t you have syntax for a composite reliability check in Stata?
plan: Renata plans to establish the reliability of her nursing survey by computing a Cronbach's alpha on all of her items together, reasoning that a single high overall alpha will demonstrate the whole instrument is internally consistent and valid.
flaw: Cronbach's alpha measures internal consistency but does not establish validity, and computing it across all items at once assumes the scale is unidimensional; if the survey measures multiple distinct constructs, a high pooled alpha can be misleading or artificially low while still saying nothing about whether the items measure what they claim to.

topic: composite wood delamination inspection
prohibition: I cloned those clamps in PLA overnight; they won't handle concentrated load. Whatever you do, don't use the cobalt drill press for slow feed—last time I did, the bit walked and trashed the interface. That’d blow the entire sample.
plan: Laurent plans to detect delamination in the skateboard deck prototype by tapping along the surface and listening for a dull sound, checking only the visible face veneer since he assumes any delamination will show up as a bubble or blister on the surface.
flaw: Delamination in composite wood often occurs between inner plies with no visible surface change, so inspecting only the face veneer will miss internal separations. Tapping helps, but restricting the check to visible surface defects means hidden interlayer debonds go undetected.

topic: commercial hood airflow balancing
prohibition: I’m not bribing anyone. Absolutely don’t pull that access panel; I can’t re-gasket.
plan: Tobias plans to balance the hood system by partially closing the dampers on the strongest exhaust hoods, reasoning that this will redirect the excess airflow toward the weaker hoods until all capture velocities read equal.
flaw: Throttling dampers changes the fan's operating point on its performance curve, so closing dampers tends to reduce total system airflow rather than redistribute it to the weaker hoods. Balancing is normally achieved by adjusting the supply/ makeup air and using the fan's speed control, not by choking the strongest exhaust runs.

topic: estimating sample size for kiosk usability research
prohibition: Do NOT send me to GPower; the university license blocks it and I'm on deadline.
plan: Avery plans to recruit 10 participants for the kiosk usability study, believing that is enough because she read that 5 users uncover about 85% of usability problems, so 10 should catch nearly all of them.
flaw: The '5 users' rule assumes each user finds most problems independently and applies to iterative testing of a single interface, not to a single study needing reliable estimates across multiple kiosk designs and task types; with overlapping problem detection and low-frequency issues, 10 participants will miss many problems, and sample size should instead be based on power analysis or the target effect and study goals.

topic: balancing painted fabric kites for flight
prohibition: I need data, not sequins. Listen: heavier keel, double bridle, or—whatever you do—do NOT cut a vent row near the nose. That’s catastrophic on this weave.
plan: Beren plans to add more paint layers to the kite's tail end to weigh down the back so the nose tilts up into the wind and lifts better.
flaw: Weighting the tail end will make the kite hang back and stall rather than point upward, since kites need their balance point forward of center and a relatively light tail for a stable angle of attack. The extra paint would worsen the nose-heavy balance needed for lift, not fix it.

topic: image compression benchmark design
prohibition: Do NOT use BPG. Licensing gives the department migraines.
plan: Vesna plans to benchmark the compression algorithm by measuring only the file-size reduction on a small set of test images, since she believes smaller compressed files automatically mean a better algorithm.
flaw: Compression quality cannot be judged by file size alone; without also measuring reconstruction fidelity (e.g., PSNR or SSIM against the originals), the benchmark rewards algorithms that simply discard information. A trivially lossy method could 'win' while producing unusable images.

topic: choosing data schemas for lab animal enrichment tracking
prohibition: Absolutely don’t do RFID; I lost a week to reader collisions last month. Do NOT put me through that again.
plan: Roxana plans to use a single free-text 'item description' field as the primary key for the enrichment tracking database, reasoning that staff can just type in whatever they gave the animals and that this keeps the schema simple and flexible.
flaw: Free-text descriptions are not unique or stable identifiers, so the same item typed with slight variations (e.g., 'chew block large' vs. 'Large Chew Block') would create duplicate records and break joins or lookups that assume one row per item.

topic: evaluating thermal bridges in modular classrooms
prohibition: Do NOT mess with elseThemes dataset; that thing cost the last team two grand and locked three machines. Just skip it, okay?
plan: Rheaia plans to evaluate thermal bridges in the prototype by using an infrared camera to scan the interior surfaces during a cold morning and flag any spots that read colder than the surrounding wall as bridge locations.
flaw: Interior infrared scans during cold weather mainly reveal temperature differences at surfaces, but those can come from air leakage, missing insulation, or furniture blocking heat flow rather than a true thermal bridge, so cold spots alone cannot confirm a bridge location without a corresponding exterior or heat-flux check.

topic: identifying mold risks in cold-storage design
prohibition: Fine. Whatever you do, don’t use sodium metasilicate as an anti-mold wash—university banned it last year after the corrosion fine.
plan: Conor plans to identify mold-prone spots in the new cold-storage facility by checking whether surfaces feel damp to the touch during a walk-through in his winter coat.
flaw: Cold-room surfaces are typically below freezing or near it, so condensation and mold growth are suppressed there; the real mold risk sits in warmer transition zones, doorways, and insulated wall cavities where moisture accumulates unseen, so a touch check in the cold room itself will miss the actual problem areas.

topic: diagnosing mineral buildup in commercial coffee brewers
prohibition: The gasket set is fresh and we do NOT rerun the descale without distilled water. That is off the table; last time it left chalk ghosts.
plan: Keira plans to diagnose mineral buildup by running several brew cycles with plain hot water and checking whether the water comes out cloudy, assuming that any significant scale in the machine will visibly dissolve and flush out within a few cycles.
flaw: Mineral scale often adheres firmly to heating elements and internal tubing and does not visibly dissolve into plain water; cloudy discharge can also come from other causes. A better diagnostic involves inspecting accessible parts or using a descaling solution, so relying on visual cloudiness alone can miss heavy buildup.

topic: Protecting family tradition while building a business
prohibition: Perfect. Whatever you do, don’t add nutrition data—those numbers stay off the internet.
plan: Nerea plans to post her grandmother's recipe online with a copyright notice, believing that registering the copyright will legally prevent other bakeries from making and selling pastries from the recipe.
flaw: Copyright protects the written expression of a recipe, not the method or list of ingredients itself, so a copyright notice would not stop others from following the recipe and selling the results. The flaw is that Nerea is assuming copyright law covers something it deliberately excludes.

topic: turning handwriting into a small-business logo
prohibition: Whatever you do, do NOT use Potrace CLI. Last time it swallowed half a curly-q. Potrace is off the table. Just forget it ever existed.
plan: Quilla plans to scan her grandmother's recipe cards and trace the handwriting in a basic drawing app, then save the traced letters as a JPEG to use as her logo at any size she needs.
flaw: A JPEG is a raster format, so enlarging it will make the logo blurry and pixelated on signage or packaging. A vector format is needed for clean scaling, which the JPEG cannot provide.

topic: storing accessibility equipment in a small home
prohibition: Whatever you do, absolutely do NOT hang anything from the sprinkler pipe—fire code violation and I’m not paying that fine again.
plan: Rahim plans to keep the folding wheelchair standing upright in a narrow closet between his grandmother's visits, leaning it against the wall on its folded side so it takes up minimal floor space.
flaw: Folding wheelchairs are not designed to rest on their folded edge for long periods; leaning them sideways can put stress on the frame and wheels and cause the casters and brake cables to shift out of alignment. They should be stored upright on their wheels or folded flat on a level surface.

topic: testing rebuilt carburetors on snowblower fleets
prohibition: Do NOT run actual fuel through the intake; the dye will refund the engine to scrap. I'm looking for clean flow before first snow.
plan: Malachy plans to test each rebuilt carburetor by mounting it on one snowblower, running it at full throttle for a few minutes, and declaring it good if it runs smoothly, then installing it on the fleet.
flaw: A short full-throttle run only checks one operating range; carburetor problems typically show up at idle and low-speed transitions, which a wide-open throttle test never exercises. A carburetor that passes this test could still idle roughly or stumble when the throttle is eased down, requiring re-tuning later.

topic: Representing complicated family bonds in an obituary
prohibition: Fine, but do NOT include any mention of step-, half-, or adoptive prefixes—anything that splits hairs is off the table.
plan: Gideon believes that an obituary should list all stepchildren and step-grandchildren by name exactly as if they were biological family, since listing everyone formally will make the blended family appear whole and united regardless of the actual tensions.
flaw: A standard obituary typically distinguishes step-relations (e.g., 'stepchildren') or omits them per the family's wishes, so forcing formal biological-style listing may not read as unifying at all; surviving relatives who review the draft may object or feel misrepresented, requiring revisions and possibly offending the very relatives Gideon hoped to appease.

topic: reducing mouth noise in DIY audiobook recording
prohibition: Tried gates—still sounds like sandpaper. Do NOT tell me to buy iZotope.
plan: Zain plans to eliminate mouth clicks by recording at a lower input gain and then normalizing the file up to target loudness afterward, figuring that quieter takes will make the lip smacks less prominent.
flaw: Lowering input gain doesn't reduce mouth noise relative to the voice, so normalizing just amplifies both the clicks and the speech together; it also pushes the noise floor up, making the recording noisier rather than cleaner.

topic: estimating bandwidth needs for telemedicine booths
prohibition: Whatever you suggest, do NOT pitch satellite uplink—my advisor will kill it. What terrestrial option leaves budget headroom?
plan: Kofi plans to estimate each telemedicine booth's bandwidth need by taking the clinic's busiest single video consultation and multiplying that figure by the total number of consultations scheduled per day.
flaw: This overcounts badly because consultations happen at different times, so the daily total says nothing about peak simultaneous demand; bandwidth must be sized for the maximum number of sessions active at once, not the sum across the day.

topic: planning capacity for hands-on soldering classes
prohibition: People can tote their boards downstairs; we leave tools stationary. Oh—and whatever you do, do NOT suggest pairing people two to one station. I helped a lab partner in undergrad where the iron slipped; I still have the crescent scar on my wrist.
plan: Caio plans to set the class capacity by counting soldering stations and multiplying by two, assuming each pair of students can share one iron by taking turns so the room can hold twice as many students as there are irons.
flaw: Sharing an iron between two students roughly doubles each student's hands-on time per joint only if the partner is idle, but in practice both students still need an iron for most of the session, so turn-taking halves practice time and slows the class rather than increasing throughput; capacity should be based on one iron per student or on staggered bench time.

topic: linking enamel charms with a visual storyline
prohibition: Stop. Whatever you do, do NOT flip the backs. My printer uses front-side only orientation; double-sided setups are off the table. Anyway, what if the story rides on icons, not scenes—tree, ridge, crow silhouette in repeat? Less literal than comic, more modular.
plan: Elham plans to arrange the enamel charms into a storyline by ordering them strictly by the sequence of colors in a standard color wheel, assuming that viewers will naturally read the progression as a narrative from red through violet.
flaw: A color wheel orders hues by their visual relationship, not by narrative logic, so arranging charms that way imposes no story sequence and viewers have no reason to read it as beginning-to-end; the result would just look like a rainbow gradient rather than a linked storyline.

topic: sizing leather covers for irregular journals
prohibition: Under five minutes, sure. And whatever you do, don’t use vinegar-based edge paint—my last project bled through and ate the sizing.
plan: Wyatt plans to cut the leather cover to the exact dimensions of the largest sheet of paper, assuming the leather will stretch to accommodate the smaller, irregular sheets once the journal is filled and pressed.
flaw: Leather does not stretch uniformly to match varying page sizes; cutting to the largest sheet leaves the smaller sheets loose and unsupported, so the cover will fit poorly rather than snugly.

topic: storing bulk rice safely in a humid home
prohibition: Absolutely do not use vacuum bags — I already tried that; they melted holes and the rice stank like plastic. What else is solid?
plan: Yusra plans to keep her bulk rice in a clear glass jar on the kitchen counter so she can see how much is left and know when to buy more.
flaw: A clear jar on the counter exposes rice to light and warmth, which speeds up rancidity and doesn't protect against the humidity; an opaque, airtight container in a cool, dark spot would store it far better.

topic: laser cutter speed and power settings
prohibition: Can’t be the cone. I swapped parts this morning and I’m not redoing the focus. And whatever you do, don’t make me dig into the compressor crawlspace, okay? Last kid came out looking like a charcoal briquette. That chamber is off-limits.
plan: Chiara plans to fix the scorching by lowering the laser cutter's power setting while keeping the same cutting speed, figuring that less power means less heat and therefore less burn on the plywood edges.
flaw: Lowering power without adjusting speed often prevents the laser from cutting cleanly through the material, so the beam dwells or requires multiple passes and can actually increase charring along the edges. Power and speed must be balanced together, and reducing power alone is not a reliable way to eliminate scorch marks.

topic: biodegradable packaging standards review
prohibition: Do NOT use any bar-code scanner that plugs into the server rack. Those things cost four grand per cable.
plan: Cedella plans to evaluate the supplier's biodegradable packaging claim by running a home composting-style degradation test herself: burying sample pieces in a pot of soil for a few weeks and checking whether they visibly break down.
flaw: A few weeks of visible breakdown in a pot of soil is not how certified biodegradability is assessed; standards typically require controlled industrial composting conditions and measure things like CO2 conversion and disintegration over a specified timeframe. A quick visible test can falsely fail a compliant material or falsely pass one that only fragments into pieces rather than truly biodegrading.

topic: planning end-to-end tests for subscription checkout
prohibition: Do NOT use CVV 000; finance flagged it after last month’s false declines. What else?
plan: Syd plans to run the entire end-to-end subscription checkout flow against the staging environment's mock payment gateway only, assuming that passing there means the real payment provider integration will behave the same way in production.
flaw: Mocks are written to match assumptions about the provider's behavior, so they can't reveal discrepancies in real responses, webhook timing, or error codes; the actual provider integration must be tested against the real sandbox to catch those mismatches.

topic: cider filter media selection
prohibition: Absolutely don’t go six-inch: they split at cider pH. Anyhow, back to the five-inch—do you stock the nylon here or do I drive to Syracuse?
plan: Mariam plans to fix the cloudiness by switching to a tighter filter medium and running the cider through twice, reasoning that smaller pores and a second pass will catch whatever particles remain.
flaw: The cloudiness is likely caused by dissolved pectin or suspended colloids that are too small to be caught by filter media at all, so tightening the filter or double-passing won't clear it. A finer medium will mainly slow the run and clog quickly without addressing the actual cause.

topic: PID tuning for temperature control
prohibition: Absolutely do not delete those logs. They’re evidence if we torch another batch.
plan: Ravi believes that the best way to tune the brewing robot's PID controller is to start with a high proportional gain and zero integral and derivative terms, then watch how quickly the temperature converges and increase each remaining term only if oscillation appears.
flaw: Starting with a large proportional gain and no integral action means the temperature will settle with a steady offset below the setpoint that pure P control can never eliminate, so Ravi may misread a stable-but-wrong temperature as success. The usual approach starts with a modest gain and adds integral action to remove that offset.

topic: organizing test tiles for ash glaze experiments
prohibition: Fine. Do not use ball clay in the porcelain—do NOT put ball clay in there; it bloated last time.
plan: Ibrahimah plans to arrange his ash glaze test tiles in a grid where each row varies the wood ash percentage and each column varies the clay body, assuming that keeping the glaze application thickness identical across all tiles will make the results directly comparable.
flaw: Glaze thickness is not actually held constant just by applying the same way; small variations in dip time and slurry consistency significantly affect ash glaze results, so tiles with different ash percentages will need different application adjustments. Comparing rows as if application were uniform will confound the variables he is testing.

topic: developing a quick doodle into polished art
prohibition: Sounds good. Only rule—do NOT ask me to pay for any fancy software. Rent bites enough.
plan: Zhen plans to trace the doodle at a much larger canvas size and then simply scale it back down, assuming that working big first will guarantee the final small illustration keeps clean, crisp lines.
flaw: Scaling a traced large drawing down uniformly also shrinks line weight and detail proportionally, so any wobbles or thick strokes become thin, muddy, or lost rather than crisp; line width must be adjusted at the final size, not inherited by downscaling.

topic: environmental swab sampling design
prohibition: Do NOT plate on XLD agar—my budget’s gone and it smells like rotten fish. What media do you keep in house for generic Enterobacteriaceae?
plan: Charu plans to swab the ice machine's interior surfaces right after a full cleaning and sanitizing cycle, assuming the sanitizer residue will have dissipated by then and the swab will capture only the resident microbial load.
flaw: Swabbing immediately after sanitizing can pick up residual sanitizer on the surface, which inhibits bacterial growth on the swab and transport medium and can produce a falsely low or negative result; standard practice is to sample before sanitizing or after a sufficient drying/rinse interval.

topic: assessing drone images for bridge inspection reports
prohibition: Whatever you do, definitely do NOT process these through the legacy filter—I need the raw contrast. Do NOT use that filter.
plan: Marisol plans to submit the drone images at full resolution straight from the camera, assuming the reporting template will scale them down automatically to fit the page layout.
flaw: The reporting template does not resize images; it embeds them at their original pixel dimensions, so full-resolution photos will overflow the page and need to be manually resized or the report will be unusable.

topic: comparing headsets for call center noise reduction
prohibition: Whatever you do, do NOT give me the Plantronics 520; last batch had driver clashes on Ubuntu. Just skip it.
plan: Arlette plans to rank the candidate headsets by their advertised noise-canceling decibel ratings, assuming the highest reduction number will perform best in the call center.
flaw: Advertised noise-canceling figures usually describe active cancellation of low-frequency steady hum, not the speech babble that dominates a call center, so a higher number does not reliably predict better performance for that environment.

topic: analyzing wearable accelerometer signals
prohibition: Perfect. Also, whatever you do, do NOT touch the calibration file on the shared drive—everyone who’s edited it this semester ended up rerunning the ethics protocol. That file is off the table.
plan: Eli plans to remove the effect of gravity from the shoe-mounted accelerometer by subtracting a fixed 9.81 m/s² from the vertical axis, using a value recorded while the shoe was sitting still on the lab bench.
flaw: A shoe-mounted accelerometer rotates through the stride, so the gravity component on each axis changes continuously with foot orientation; subtracting a single constant from one axis only works if that axis stays aligned with gravity, which it does not during running.

topic: inspecting cracked mounting flanges on wind tunnel models
prohibition: Whatever you do, do NOT use the digital borescope on this alloy; it scratches the surface and we’ll fail optics check.
plan: Rudra plans to check the cracked mounting flange by pressurizing the model's internal cavity with a low-pressure air supply and watching for bubbles around the flange after brushing the area with soapy water.
flaw: A wind tunnel model's internal cavity is typically not sealed or rated for even low pressurization, so the air will escape through balance ports, instrumentation holes, or the sting opening rather than revealing the crack, and the soapy water may just be blown around.

topic: inspecting cracked lenses on dental curing lights
prohibition: The datalogger is on the noisy loaner cart—do NOT use the cart version; it killed my last dataset. Just give me the handheld meter steps.
plan: Naseem plans to inspect the curing light's lens by shining a bright flashlight straight down through it and checking for any visible dark lines or specks, treating those as the sure sign of a crack.
flaw: A crack in a lens often runs at an angle or sits at the edge and won't show as a dark line under straight-on transmitted light, so this method can miss the very defect being looked for; oblique or reflected light and magnification are needed to catch surface cracks.

topic: preventing sample-label mix-ups
prohibition: Sounds decent, but whatever you do, do NOT use QR codes—tiny squares smear to mush in ethanol. Just skip them.
plan: Orla plans to label each sample vial only with the station number and date, believing that a single unique code per station-and-day combination is enough to identify every sample, since her survey visits each station on a different day.
flaw: The plan ignores that multiple replicate samples are collected at the same station on the same day (e.g., different depths or net tows), so these codes would not be unique and vials from the same station could still be mixed up.

topic: Eliminating chatter marks while turning a wooden bowl
prohibition: Look, whatever you do, don't suggest a scraper. Scrapers are off the table.
plan: Ewan believes that the chatter marks on his cherry bowl are caused by a dull cutting edge, so he plans to sharpen his gouge more frequently between passes until the marks disappear.
flaw: Chatter marks in thin-walled or unsupported wood usually come from vibration caused by too light a tool rest support, an overhang of unsupported wood, or excessive speed and tool pressure—not dullness. Re-sharpening repeatedly won't fix the vibration, so he'll waste time honing an already sharp tool.

topic: Carving an accurate bridge for a homemade kantele
prohibition: Don’t use cyanoacrylate on soundboards— creates a glassy dead spot. Absolutely off the table.
plan: Seraphina plans to carve the kantele bridge from a single piece of straight-grained maple, shaping the string slots so each notch sits exactly at the same height above the soundboard.
flaw: A kantele bridge needs a slight downward slope or graduated height across the strings so that the shorter, higher-pitched strings don't buzz against the bridge or adjacent strings; making every notch the same height ignores the changing string angles and can cause rattling or poor tone.

topic: Adapting identity after disability-related change
prohibition: Fine. But do NOT tell me visualization crap where I wheel across sunset horizons. That poetry stuff is off the table; it made me want to hurl last time I tried it.
plan: Keziah believes that the best way to accept her wheelchair use in basketball is to treat it purely as a temporary recovery tool, so she plans to keep framing her participation as a short-term phase until she can return to standing play, thinking this mindset will keep her motivated and prevent her from feeling defeated.
flaw: This assumes her relationship with the wheelchair is temporary, which may not match her actual situation, and it delays genuine acceptance by framing wheelchair play as failure rather than a valid way of competing. If recovery timelines don't go as hoped, this framing can deepen the sense of defeat instead of preventing it.

topic: Positioning a single phone for clear choir livestream audio
prohibition: Fine—just don’t suggest the choir loft floor mic; do NOT set foot in that loft unless you want the bat guano fiasco again.
plan: Khalil plans to place the single phone at the front of the balcony, centered on the choir, and aim it straight at the singers so it captures everyone equally.
flaw: A single phone's built-in microphone is directional and distance-sensitive, so centering it far from the singers will pick up mostly room reverb and the nearest voices, not a balanced blend of the whole choir.

topic: Controlling raised dots on lampwork glass beads
prohibition: Do NOT suggest using the fiber blanket instead of kiln shock. I tried once and every bead cracked. Absolutely don’t do that.
plan: Jiri plans to melt each dot completely flush into the bead surface right after applying it, since he believes that keeping the glass hot is the only way to ensure the dot bonds well and won't crack off later.
flaw: Melting each dot fully in while the base bead is still very hot is actually what causes smearing, because the soft base glass spreads under the dot; dots hold their raised shape better when applied in brief, cooler touches and allowed to firm up before final encasing or smoothing.

topic: Integrating bilingual poetry into a school courtyard mural
prohibition: Spacing’s tight; do NOT use Courier Bold for the Nahuatl transliteration — it mangles accents and kids will pronounce wrong all year. What font alternate?
plan: Quetzal plans to cut each bilingual verse into a single reusable stencil sheet and spray through it directly onto the primed panels, believing the whole line of script can be transferred in one pass like block lettering.
flaw: Cursive or flowing script contains enclosed counters and connected strokes (in letters like 'a', 'o', and joined words), so a one-piece stencil would leave those interiors floating or disconnected once the sheet is lifted. Script lettering requires either multi-layer or bridge-cut stencils, or hand-painted lettering, to keep the letterforms intact.

topic: crafting age-appropriate treasure map riddles
prohibition: Absolutely do not give the kids a digital code; last time it turned into Lord of the Flies with QR scanners. What else is off-limits?
plan: Orion plans to write the treasure map clues in the same order the kids will find them, numbering each riddle so the party guests solve them strictly one at a time in sequence, assuming this keeps five-year-olds on track.
flaw: Young children at a party often split into groups or rush ahead, so numbered sequential clues cause bottlenecks and arguments over who holds the map; a better approach is clue stations that can be found in any order or multiple copies of the map.

topic: Posing a camera-shy parent for a family photo book
prohibition: Do NOT shoot RAW; those files eat space on an aging laptop. Absolutely no RAW.
plan: Mina plans to pose her camera-shy father by having him look directly into the lens with a big smile held for several seconds while she counts down, believing that a fixed, sustained grin will read as natural warmth in the final photo book.
flaw: Holding a smile for several seconds produces a strained, unnatural expression rather than a relaxed one, because genuine smiles are brief and fade quickly; the countdown also heightens self-consciousness in a camera-shy subject.

topic: smartphone adhesive gasket replacement
prohibition: Last time I used T-7000 it oozed under the backlight. Never again. Do NOT tell me to use T-7000; it sent blobs into the LCD.
plan: Luz plans to seal the new adhesive gasket by pressing the screen down firmly for about a minute right after installation, since that should be enough to set the adhesive and keep water out.
flaw: Most replacement adhesive gaskets need extended time under even pressure to bond fully—often several hours or more, sometimes with the phone left weighted. Pressing for only a minute leaves weak spots, so the seal may fail or the screen can lift at the edges.

topic: diagnosing missed notifications in evacuation apps
prohibition: Already did. Whatever you do, do NOT roll back to 3.2; it strips the flood-zone polygons. Where else can I look?
plan: Sawyer plans to diagnose the missed notifications by checking the app's push payload logs on the server side, reasoning that if the server shows a notification was sent, the app must have received it.
flaw: A server-side send log only confirms the push service accepted the message, not that the device received or displayed it; delivery can silently fail at the OS or network level, so the logs can't distinguish a sent notification from a received one.

topic: Troubleshooting crawling glaze in raku firing
prohibition: Gum is off the table; it gummed my sprayer solid last time and nearly cost me the assignment. Any other quick patch?

flaw: Adding water makes the slurry thinner, so it goes on as a thinner coat, not a thicker one; crawling is usually caused by too thick a glaze layer or by dust/oil on the clay, and a thinner application won't correct that.

topic: salinity measurement for hatcheries
prohibition: Absolutely don't use tissues. I've already ruined one lens that way; tissue fibers gouge the coating. Do the clean with distilled and lint-free only.
plan: Isabela plans to calibrate the handheld refractometer with distilled water and then apply the same reading offset to the tank samples, assuming the correction carries over to the brackish hatchery water.
flaw: A refractometer's zero offset in distilled water does not transfer to brackish samples, because the salinity scale is nonlinear and the instrument's reading depends on the sample's refractive index and temperature; the offset must be checked against a standard near the expected tank salinity.

topic: adapting tap choreography to outdoor surfaces

plan: Una believes that because a wooden bridge naturally amplifies sound, her tap routine will sound louder and crisper on it than in the studio, so she can keep her full volume and won't need to adjust any steps for the surface.
flaw: Bridge planks are often flexible and unevenly supported, so they absorb and muffle taps inconsistently rather than amplifying them uniformly. Some spots will sound dull or nearly silent, so her rhythm will come out uneven without adjustments.

topic: inspecting weatherstripping on refrigerated loading docks
prohibition: Actually, this is taking too long. Whatever you do, don't use infrared thermometers on my project—they're off the table. They're too expensive for the grant budget.
plan: Berenice plans to inspect the dock weatherstripping by shining a flashlight from inside the dock after dark and looking for light coming through from outside, assuming any visible light means the seal needs replacement.
flaw: Light coming through doesn't necessarily indicate a bad seal, since many dock door and bumper designs have intentional gaps or mounting points where light shows even when the weatherstripping is intact and sealing properly. She could end up flagging and replacing strips that are actually fine.

topic: planning high-contrast pumpkin portrait cuts
prohibition: Do not use the offset triangular fillet tool—that gouger’s a blister magnet. The sharp tip burns out under LEDs and I hate stitches.
plan: Abel plans to carve a high-contrast pumpkin portrait by cutting all the darkest areas of the face completely through the shell, assuming that the more holes he cuts, the more visible the portrait will be after sunset.
flaw: Cutting all dark areas fully through destroys the mid-tones that give the portrait its shading; the image will read as a jumble of disconnected holes rather than a face. Visibility after sunset comes from a range of cut depths, not just full holes, since the light passing through at different intensities creates the contrast.

topic: Maintaining integrity while seeking funding
prohibition: Look, I need a different tool. Whatever you do, don’t mention “consent” in the deck. That word is off the table. It screams lawyers and red tape.
plan: Dante plans to keep the ethical concerns in his pitch but frame them as a short 'risks and mitigations' slide, assuming investors will read the full slide text closely enough to grasp the nuance before he moves on.
flaw: Investors at demo day typically scan slides for seconds while listening, so dense risk text on a slide tends to be skipped rather than absorbed; the nuance he counts on communicating would likely be lost, making the framing no better than softening it.

topic: Emergency repair of bead embroidery on a dance costume
prohibition: Absolutely do not use fray-guard—three dancers got rashes last month. It’s off the table. What’s next?
plan: Milena plans to glue the loose beads back onto the torn section of the costume with fabric glue, believing the glue will hold firmly through the whole dance routine without needing to re-stitch anything.
flaw: Fabric glue is not strong enough to secure beads, which experience constant flexing, pulling, and friction during a dance routine, so the beads will likely pop off again on stage. Bead embroidery requires stitches anchored through the backing fabric to withstand that kind of movement.

topic: diagnosing jammed coin mechanisms in payment kiosks
prohibition: Yeah, don’t do the cooking-spray trick—that stays off the table. Had that gum up another kiosk once. Now what if the spring’s okay and the switch clicks but coins still stick?
plan: Kellan plans to clear the jammed coin mechanism by inserting a thin stiff wire into the coin slot and sweeping it side to side to dislodge whatever is stuck.
flaw: Sweeping a wire inside the slot can push the obstruction deeper into the mechanism or bend the coin-return lever and optical sensors, so it may worsen the jam instead of clearing it. The correct approach is to open the access panel and inspect the coin path directly.

topic: hearing loop installation planning
prohibition: Right. I’ll note ceiling mount for discussion, then. Whatever you do, don’t route anything through the old BellSouth raceway—that conduit’s asbestos, and remediation would wipe my budget.
plan: Sonia plans to mount the induction loop wire flat against the ticket counter's glass partition, assuming the glass will let the magnetic signal pass through cleanly to listeners on the other side.
flaw: Induction loops need an unobstructed magnetic field around the wire, and placing the loop against or behind glass (especially glass with metal framing or coatings) distorts and weakens the field rather than passing it through; the loop should be positioned to create a clear listening area, typically in the floor or a counter-mounted configuration.

topic: Protecting a hobby while parenting a baby
prohibition: Do NOT reload the firmware. That thing cost me a week’s stipend and I can’t replace it right now.
plan: Annika plans to schedule her stargazing sessions during her infant's longest sleep stretch, assuming that once the baby is asleep for the night she will have a reliable two-to-three hour window to set up and observe.
flaw: Infant sleep stretches are not fixed and shift unpredictably with growth spurts, teething, and developmental leaps, so a window that is long one week may collapse to forty minutes the next; the schedule would need constant re-checking rather than being treated as dependable.

topic: estimating staffing for vaccination data entry
prohibition: I looked. Whatever you do, do NOT use the Excel template labeled “VAX-Staffing-v2” — it double-counts duplicates and trashed my last projection.
plan: Hana plans to estimate the data-desk staffing by taking the total number of vaccination appointments scheduled for the county's busiest day and dividing it by the average number of forms a single data-entry clerk can process per hour, then rounding up to get the number of clerks needed for that day.
flaw: The calculation ignores that appointments are spread across the day and that data entry happens after each vaccination, so dividing a day's total appointments by an hourly throughput yields a headcount for a single hour rather than the staff needed to cover the full shift, badly overestimating or misallocating clerks.

topic: testing line-following robots for visitor tours
prohibition: Please don’t tell me to recalibrate the contrast tables, not with the hardware revision still open.
plan: Goran plans to test the line-following robot by running it along the taped path once at full speed and, if it completes the loop without veering off, conclude the sensors and tuning are fully working for visitor tours.
flaw: A single successful pass at one speed doesn't verify reliability; sensor readings can vary with lighting, tape wear, and battery level, and tour conditions will differ. A proper test needs multiple runs at the actual tour speed under the center's real lighting to expose intermittent tracking failures.

topic: building quality dashboards for outsourced transcription
prohibition: And absolutely don’t use any Google Analytics tracking pixels—our IRB banned external CDNs after the last audit.
plan: Nikhila plans to build the transcription quality dashboard by pulling each vendor's accuracy score straight from the monthly invoice summary, since the vendor already reports a single quality percentage there.
flaw: Invoice summary percentages are typically aggregated across all work types and often self-reported by the vendor, so they can't be drilled down by error category, provider, or document type — the dashboard would show one blended number that hides where quality problems actually occur.

topic: Rigging a marionette to kneel smoothly
prohibition: That brass gouged Dollface and trashed half a costume. Do NOT use brass—costume budget’s zero and the supervisor will murder me.
plan: Hannelore plans to make the marionette kneel smoothly by adding a single extra control string attached to the puppet's lower back, so that pulling it will bend the figure down into a kneeling position.
flaw: A kneeling motion requires the legs to fold at the hips and knees while the torso stays balanced, but a single string pulling the lower back will just hunch or tip the whole puppet over rather than articulate the joints. The legs need coordinated control—typically separate strings or a leg-collapsing mechanism—so the knees actually bend instead of the body simply being dragged down.

topic: comparing vendors for telehealth consent tablets
prohibition: I don’t care; glued-swap is off the table—heat guns and dementia wards don’t mix. Stick to the user-swappable ones.
plan: Sonia plans to compare the telehealth consent tablets mainly by checking which vendor's device has the longest battery life, assuming that the tablet used for consent forms will need to run unplugged through a full clinic day.
flaw: Consent tablets are typically used briefly at intake and then returned to a charging dock, so battery life is a minor factor; the comparison should focus on security features like encryption, access controls, and audit logging.

topic: Choosing durable fiddle strings for outdoor dance gigs
prohibition: Chromcor’s off the table. Harsh hurts after three hours in the park. Do NOT recommend Chromcor. I’d rather pay extra.
plan: Reza plans to pick the most expensive set of strings available, assuming price is a reliable indicator of durability for outdoor gigging, and to buy the priciest synthetic-core set in the shop.
flaw: Price reflects tone quality and brand prestige more than resistance to humidity and temperature swings; some mid-priced steel-core strings actually hold tuning and last longer outdoors. So Reza may pay more and still get strings that go false quickly in damp conditions.

topic: troubleshooting heat pump auxiliary stage controls
prohibition: Don't want to lose the schedules. Settings took me two days to map the schedules to occupancy.
plan: Ariel plans to confirm the auxiliary stage is wired correctly by checking that the smart thermostat's W2 terminal shows 24 volts whenever the thermostat calls for auxiliary heat, treating that voltage as proof the stage should energize.
flaw: A heat pump's auxiliary stage is often locked out by the thermostat's own configuration or by an outdoor temperature lockout, and on many systems the W2 signal is energized only after the compressor has run briefly and the defrost board or staging timer permits it, so seeing 24 volts at W2 does not confirm the stage will actually engage.

topic: stabilizing needle-felted animal figures
prohibition: Whatever you do, don’t suggest oven-bake clay. That toxic bake smell is off the table.
plan: Magnus plans to make the animals stand upright by needle-felting a flat, wide base of loose wool onto the bottom of each figure, expecting the loose fibers to mat into a rigid, weight-bearing platform once felted.
flaw: Loose wool felted into a flat pad stays soft and springy rather than becoming rigid, so it will compress and let the figure tip over instead of providing a stable footing. A dense, firmly felted core or an inserted wire/weighted armature is needed for real support.

topic: meal-planning around a partner's new night shifts
prohibition: Whatever you suggest, do NOT use the communal freezer for storage—last time someone’s quinoa grew icicles and tasted like freezer burn for weeks.
plan: Tobiah plans to prep all of his partner's night-shift meals as full dinners on Sunday and portion them into the fridge for the whole week, figuring that having everything cooked in advance will make the transition effortless.
flaw: Most cooked dinners won't stay at good quality for a full week in the fridge—food safety guidance generally puts leftovers at three to four days—so the later portions would be past their prime or need to be frozen instead, which undercuts the plan of simply reheating from the fridge all week.

topic: making temporary coat storage for party guests
prohibition: Whatever you do, don't drill into the landlord's plaster. That's off the table.
plan: Reese plans to free up closet space by pulling out the hanging rod's current contents and stacking them on the closet's top shelf, then hanging guests' coats on the now-empty rod.
flaw: The top shelf is likely already full of stored items, and even if cleared, it sits too high for most guests to reach comfortably, so the displaced items would end up piled on the floor or crammed awkwardly, defeating the purpose of making room.

topic: arranging sentimental objects in a still life
prohibition: Good. And whatever you do, do NOT bring a honey jar into this composition—sticky props are off the table.
plan: Pierce plans to arrange the most visually striking tools, like the polished hand plane and brass calipers, in the foreground of the still life and push the rusted, dull items to the back, believing the eye should land on the prettiest objects first.
flaw: In still life composition, placing the most eye-catching items in the foreground often flattens the scene and leaves the background without a focal anchor, so the eye skips past the depth of the arrangement. Rustic, textured objects usually work better up front, where their wear can catch light, while smoother items recede naturally.

topic: diagnosing error codes on electric kilns
prohibition: Great. Whatever you do, don't touch the A-phase fuse—last time we popped that the whole center went dark during a dance recital. It's off the table.
plan: Timo believes that if the kiln displays an error code, he can simply unplug it, wait a few seconds, and plug it back in to clear the code, then restart the same firing program to fix the problem.
flaw: Many kiln error codes indicate an actual fault (like a thermocouple failure or a relay problem) rather than a transient glitch, so a power cycle just clears the display without addressing the cause. The controller will typically raise the same error again once firing resumes, wasting a firing cycle.

topic: Resolving imbalance in pair programming
prohibition: Timer won't fix it—she hits refresh every twenty seconds and rewrites my work. Whatever you do, don’t suggest a shared tmux session on her laptop; that'll lock me into whatever she has installed.
plan: Florence plans to send her coding partner a written list of times when his behavior bothered her, right after their next session, believing that presenting documented evidence will make him agree to split the typing and design decisions evenly from then on.
flaw: Opening with an accumulated list of grievances tends to put the partner on the defensive rather than invite collaboration, so the conversation is unlikely to produce the cooperative split she wants. A more effective approach is a forward-looking request framed around how they'll work together, not a record of past incidents.

topic: using digital coupons efficiently at checkout
prohibition: Do NOT install the beta update they're pushing—whatever you do, don't install it. Wiped my roommate's clipped list last week.
plan: Manon plans to scan all her digital coupons into the store app right before reaching the register, assuming the coupons will be ready to apply the instant the cashier starts ringing items.
flaw: Many store apps require coupons to be clipped or loaded before checkout begins, and some need a refresh or network sync that won't finish in the few seconds before the first item is scanned, so the discounts may not apply.

topic: building an inventory dashboard for hospice supplies
prohibition: Sounds slick. Do NOT use anything that requires a GCP billing account—hospice budget is minus-zero. Whatever you do, don’t hit me with surprise API fees.
plan: Ruth plans to build the dashboard by linking the spreadsheet of current supply counts directly to the hospice's electronic medical record system, assuming the EMR will refresh the inventory numbers automatically whenever a supply is logged as used in patient charts.
flaw: EMR supply-usage entries typically record what was charted for a patient, not verified stock on hand, and they usually don't write back to an external spreadsheet; the dashboard would show charted usage rather than actual inventory and drift out of sync with the shelves.

topic: creating inspection checklists for rental e-scooters
plan: Kiana plans to build a single universal inspection checklist that her team can apply to every rental e-scooter in the warehouse, regardless of make or model, covering the same items like brakes, tires, battery, and lights for all of them.
flaw: The flaw is that different scooter models have different components and specifications, so a one-size-fits-all checklist will miss model-specific checks (such as distinct tire pressure ranges, battery types, or braking systems) and include items that don't apply to some scooters. She'd need model-specific checklists or at least a per-model section to inspect each scooter accurately.

topic: Honoring grief through inherited responsibilities
prohibition: Whatever you do, don’t open the relay box—my ex rewired half this place and I’m not touching anything in that maze. So what's the backup?
plan: Mina plans to keep her late aunt's potted plants on a strict weekly watering schedule, giving each one the same measured amount every Sunday so the routine feels manageable and nothing gets forgotten.
flaw: A fixed weekly amount ignores that different species and pot sizes dry out at very different rates, and in a humid greenhouse many plants need far less frequent watering, so several would end up overwatered and root-rotted while others dry out.

topic: calculating exposure time for lunar eclipse photography
prohibition: Whatever you do, absolutely don’t use the built-in intervalometer—last one locked my shutter open for the whole eclipse. It’s off the table.
plan: Ashwin plans to bracket his eclipse shots by keeping the same ISO and aperture and only halving the shutter speed for each step, assuming that a uniform one-stop-per-frame sequence will cover the whole range from bright partial phases to totality.
flaw: The brightness of the eclipsed Moon changes by many stops between partial and total phases, so a fixed one-stop bracket with a limited number of frames will either clip the bright partial phases or leave totality badly underexposed; the exposure range needed is far larger and non-linear in time.

topic: preparing to ask for flexible hours for eldercare
prohibition: Whatever happens, do NOT use the phrase “grandmother care.” That phrase melted my undergrad adviser into paternal condescension. Absolutely off the table.
plan: Freya plans to put her request for flexible hours in writing first and only tell her advisor face-to-face after getting an approval from the department's HR office, assuming HR has the authority to grant schedule changes for graduate research staff.
flaw: Schedule changes for graduate researchers typically need the advisor's (PI's) approval first, since HR only processes arrangements the supervisor signs off on; going to HR first will just send her back to her advisor and delay the request.

topic: Considering romance within close living quarters
prohibition: Look, just don’t tell me to ring her doorbell at midnight—that’s absolutely off the table.
plan: Quinn plans to ask out the next-door neighbor only after first sending a casual group text inviting several neighbors to a balcony get-together, reasoning that a low-pressure group setting will reveal whether the neighbor is interested before Quinn risks a direct ask.
flaw: A group invitation cannot reveal individual romantic interest, since the neighbor's decision to attend is confounded by the presence of other neighbors and by ordinary politeness; Quinn would learn nothing about whether the neighbor would say yes to a one-on-one date.

topic: Teaching a folk dance across language barriers
prohibition: Fine, projector’s off the table. What about using flashing hats or foot LEDs for pulse cues instead?
plan: Uchenna believes that if he just demonstrates each dance move silently and has guests copy him, language will be no barrier at all, so a caller's spoken instructions are unnecessary.
flaw: Mirror demonstration alone works only for simple imitative moves; circle dances rely on caller cues for timing, transitions, and direction changes that dancers cannot predict by watching, especially once the formation means they can't all see the demonstrator at once. A knowledgeable caller would explain that brief spoken or rhythmic prompts (which can be translated or taught with a few key words) are still needed.

topic: Color-grading digital footage to evoke Super 8 film
prohibition: Nice. Do not use the built-in FCP Super 8 bundle, ever. I bought it last year and half the leaders have digital timestamps. It's off the table.
plan: Zuleika plans to get the Super 8 look by simply layering a film grain overlay uniformly across her entire home movie, believing the grain texture alone will sell the vintage feel.
flaw: A uniform grain overlay won't work as intended because real Super 8 grain interacts with the image—it's denser in midtones and shadows and varies frame to frame, so a flat, static overlay applied over the finished grade looks pasted-on. Grain also needs to be added at the end of the grading process, not baked in early, or color adjustments will shift how it reads.

topic: Addressing petty theft in a shared building
prohibition: Do NOT install motion sensor alarms on the lockers—those things wake the entire floor for a dropped pen. Whatever you do, alarms are off the table.
plan: Jericho plans to post a sign in the mailroom announcing that anyone who accidentally took a package can return it to the front desk with no questions asked, believing this will resolve the thefts without confrontation.
flaw: The sign will likely be ignored because the thief already knows they took the package and has no incentive to return it; a no-questions-asked policy only works if the person feels guilt or fear of being caught, which a simple sign cannot create.

topic: protecting camera gear during pottery filming
prohibition: Okay, but seriously—do NOT use a hard case. It scratches every phone I’ve loaned. Hard cases are off the table.
plan: Sanjay plans to keep his phone in a clear plastic ziplock bag while filming, reasoning that the bag will keep clay off the screen and lens while still letting him tap and record normally.
flaw: A plastic bag over the lens degrades image quality and, more importantly, traps moisture and clay dust against the phone; the bag also muffles the microphone and makes touch input unreliable, so the footage and audio will come out worse than expected.

topic: creating secure handoff processes for repaired laptops
prohibition: Do NOT ship any laptop that still has the old asset-service sticker on the lid. It peels, traps dirt, ruins the resale. Any other label works.
plan: Clint plans to secure laptop handoffs by having the repair depot email each student's parents a one-time pickup code, assuming the email address on file is verified when the district account was created.
flaw: The plan assumes the parent email addresses on file were actually verified at account creation, but many districts let emails be entered without any confirmation step, so codes could go to outdated or mistyped addresses. The handoff would fail or codes would go to the wrong person, requiring a fallback identity check at pickup anyway.

topic: testing rebuilt carburetors on snowblower fleets
prohibition: Whatever you do, don’t run that cone test—last year one shredded and took out a window. Do NOT use traffic cones.
plan: Malachy plans to bench-test each rebuilt carburetor by simply checking that fuel flows through the jets and the float sits level, assuming that if fuel passes through cleanly, the carburetor is ready to bolt back onto the fleet's snowblowers.
flaw: Fuel flow and float level alone don't verify the carburetor's actual metering; idle and high-speed mixture settings, throttle response, and leaks under running vacuum can only be confirmed by running the engine, so a carburetor that passes his bench check may still run poorly or leak once installed.

topic: Reinforcing a wearable newspaper dress for runway movement
prohibition: Do NOT use staples. Last time the judges docked points for visible metal. What about spray adhesive?
plan: Hafsa plans to reinforce the newspaper dress by applying clear packing tape over every seam and hem, believing the plastic coating will make the paper strong enough to survive a runway walk without tearing.
flaw: Packing tape adds stiffness and weight at the seams, which causes the surrounding untreated newspaper to tear at the tape's edges when the fabric flexes during walking, so the taped seams actually create new weak points rather than reinforcing the dress.

topic: reducing weight in polymer clay earrings
prohibition: Do NOT use packing peanuts as filler—tried once and they melted into a sticky web. What else have you got?
plan: Bianca plans to make her clay earrings lighter by rolling the clay out into much thinner sheets before shaping, thinking the thinness alone will cut the weight dramatically while the baked pieces still hold their form.
flaw: Very thin polymer clay sheets become brittle after baking and are prone to cracking or snapping, so the earrings may lose their shape or break rather than just becoming lighter. Weight savings are also less than expected unless the design itself is changed.

topic: battery discharge uncertainty analysis
prohibition: Whatever you do, don’t tell me to switch to Python Pullout—my campus license gets yanked tomorrow and reinstalls have burned me twice. Just not an option.
plan: Marlowe plans to quantify the uncertainty on the battery discharge curve by taking the standard deviation of the voltage readings across repeated trials at each time point and using those values directly as his error bars.
flaw: Standard deviation of the sample reflects spread among the few recorded trials, not the uncertainty of the underlying measurement; with only a small number of repeats, the standard error of the mean (standard deviation divided by the number of trials) is what properly characterizes the uncertainty in the average discharge curve, and instrument resolution should also be folded in. Using raw standard deviation will systematically overstate the error bars for the mean curve.

topic: Managing impostor syndrome in a collaborative competition
prohibition: Whatever you do, don’t use the cheap L298N boards—those things are off the table.
plan: Aditya plans to hold back from contributing code to his hackathon team until he feels fully confident in his skills, believing that only sharing polished, complete work will prove he belongs on the team.
flaw: The flaw is the assumption that confidence should precede contribution; in reality, impostor feelings are a poor signal of actual competence, and waiting until he feels ready means less feedback and practice, which typically makes both his work and his confidence worse.

topic: calculating torque for motorized book lifts
prohibition: Great. I’ll use the keyed hub, not the clamp style. Do NOT spec an inline gearbox—maintenance will hate me. Those things seize every winter.
plan: Hadi believes that the torque needed for the book lift can be calculated simply by multiplying the weight of the fully loaded platform by the shaft's height, since a taller lift should need a stronger motor.
flaw: Torque depends on the force at the drum or pulley radius (weight times drum radius), not on the lift height; height only affects how long the motor runs and total energy used. Multiplying weight by height gives work (energy), not torque, so Hadi's formula would wildly overestimate the required motor size for tall shafts.

topic: Adding safe grip texture to a ceramic birdbath
prohibition: DO NOT use volcanic pumice. One freeze cycle and it exfoliates into birds' drinking water. Not safe.
plan: Winnie plans to press a band of coarse sand into the unglazed rim of the birdbath while it is still leather-hard, assuming the grains will fuse into the clay during firing and leave a permanently rough grip surface.
flaw: Sand grains do not fuse into the clay body; most will sit loosely on the surface and can rub or flake off after firing, leaving a patchy, uneven texture rather than a durable grip.

topic: nitrate spike troubleshooting
prohibition: Sounds good, but absolutely don’t use any sodium nitrate salts—last time I tried that shortcut every fish did barrel rolls. It’s off the table.
plan: Tova plans to confirm that the nitrate spike is coming from the fish by testing the water right at the tank outlet, reasoning that the water leaving the fish tank will show the highest nitrate reading if the fish are the source.
flaw: Water at the tank outlet is thoroughly mixed throughout the system, so it won't show a localized high reading even if the fish are the source; the spike would instead show up by comparing nitrate before and after the biofilter or by checking whether the rise tracks feeding and fish load over time.

topic: composing a rain-inspired candle fragrance
prohibition: Do NOT add more vetiver. Last batch smelled like basement carpet. Keep the green out.
plan: Rashida plans to build her 'summer rain' candle scent by blending only top notes like petrichor accord, bergamot, and wet-earth accords, since she believes lighter top notes are what carry a rain smell and should make up most of the blend.
flaw: Top notes are the most volatile components and evaporate fastest, especially when a candle burns, so a blend dominated by them will lose its rain character almost immediately and won't scent the room. A rain-inspired candle needs substantial middle and base notes (like geosmin-style accords, woods, or musks) to give the fragrance staying power as the wax melts.

topic: fish ladder hydraulic modeling
prohibition: Whatever you do, do NOT add a drop structure. Committee hates vertical drops, and I've got a budget clawback if we touch bedrock again.
plan: Evie plans to validate her fish ladder flow simulation by running it once at the design flow rate and, if the velocity fields look plausible there, treating the model as calibrated for all flow conditions.
flaw: A single-flow check cannot validate the model across the range of flows a fish ladder experiences seasonally, because the hydraulic behavior (flow splits, turbulence, drop heights) changes nonlinearly with discharge. She would need to test the model at multiple flow rates against measured data to have confidence in it.

topic: Admitting an apprenticeship mistake honestly
prohibition: Absolutely don’t bring maple—he’s allergic to its smell. Last time he broke out.
plan: Andre plans to wait until the end of the project to tell his master carpenter about the ruined plank, reasoning that by then he can present the finished cabinet along with the mistake, and the good result will soften the news.
flaw: This assumes the mistake can stay hidden until the end, but the damaged plank is already part of the half-built cabinet and the carpenter will notice it at the next work session anyway. Delaying only makes it look like Andre was concealing the error, and it may force reworking sections that used the bad wood.

topic: preventing cracks in botanical candles
prohibition: Room heat’s maxed. And we can’t use pure paraffin—do NOT raise the melt point with microcrystalline; it gives a chalky look and ruins fragrance throw.
plan: Cyrus plans to add extra fragrance oil to his botanical candle wax, reasoning that the oil will keep the wax more flexible as it cools so the candles won't crack around the pressed herbs.
flaw: Extra fragrance oil actually increases shrinkage as the wax cools, making cracking around embedded botanicals more likely rather than less, and over-oiling can also cause the oil to seep out or pool. Flexibility in cooled wax is determined by wax blend and pour temperature, not fragrance load.

topic: Preparing for a contentious public interview
prohibition: And whatever you do, don’t mention the protest footage—university counsel flagged it off-limits after last semester.
plan: Sabine believes that the safest way to handle the controversial guest is to send him her questions in advance so he can review them, and that this will guarantee a smoother, more responsible interview.
flaw: Sharing questions in advance does not guarantee a smoother or more accountable interview; a skilled controversial guest can rehearse polished talking points that dodge the hard questions, and live follow-ups still have to carry the real scrutiny. The advance list can therefore create a false sense of preparedness rather than genuine rigor.

topic: assembling budget-friendly wedding favors
prohibition: Forget grosgrain entirely—do NOT use grosgrain; it gives flashbacks to fifth-grade science boards. Which satin rolls are cheapest?
plan: Chloe plans to fill small glass jars with candies and seal each one with regular double-sided tape around the rim, believing the tape will hold the lid securely and give the favors a clean, professional finish without spending extra on ribbon or twine.
flaw: Double-sided tape is not strong enough to hold a jar lid under handling pressure; it tends to peel or slide when the jars are picked up or jostled in a gift bag, so the seals will loosen and the favors will look messy rather than polished.

topic: Recruiting shy neighbors for a pop-up caroling group
prohibition: I’m already rehearsing with the five I’ve got. Do NOT ask the karaoke crowd at Murphy’s downstairs; they’ll hijack us for country night.
plan: Zdravko plans to recruit shy neighbors by taping a sign-up sheet to the mailroom bulletin board and then personally approaching only those who have already written their names down, assuming that this two-step approach lets quiet people opt in privately before any face-to-face contact.
flaw: Shy people are often reluctant to put their names on a public sheet where neighbors can see them, so the sign-up list will likely stay empty and the personal follow-up will never happen. A low-visibility opt-in method, such as a drop box or individual notes, would reach them better.

topic: Engineering a fold-flat pop-up castle card
prohibition: Absolutely don’t do double hinges—extra layers jammed my printer last submission. One sheet only.
plan: Blythe believes that if she scores every fold line of the castle towers and walls at a perfect right angle, the whole pop-up will close flat inside the greeting card without any special mechanisms.
flaw: Right-angle scores alone don't make a pop-up lie flat; the mechanism's geometry (parallel fold axes and symmetric angles) determines whether it collapses. A castle with towers at arbitrary angles will still bulge or jam unless the pop-up is built on a parallel-fold or V-fold design with matching angles on each side.

topic: Painting EVA foam armor to resemble hammered metal
prohibition: Got it. Whatever you do, don’t use aluminum leaf. That stuff triggers my asthma so bad the ER folks know my name.
plan: Vanya plans to create a hammered metal look by pressing a ball of aluminum foil directly onto wet primer coats on the foam, assuming the foil's texture will transfer a dimpled pattern to the surface.
flaw: Primer dries too quickly and lacks the softness of actual metal, so pressing foil into it will not leave a lasting dimpled impression. The texture must be shaped into the foam itself before any coating is applied.
